evidence: Cic. Planc. 33: cum ille eum salūtāsset, ut fit (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The everyday word, of saying salvē or avē to someone, in every period. With a second accusative, to hail someone as something: Caesarem salūtāre. The noun salūtātiō is a greeting, and also the morning call on a patron (Cic. Fam. 9.20.3).

evidence: Cic. de Or. 2.13: cum inter sē … amīcissimē cōnsalūtāssent (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: pater familiās, ubi ad vīllam vēnit, ubi larem familiārem salūtāvit, fundum eōdem diē, sī potest, circumeat
phrases.english: the master, when he comes to the farm and has greeted the god of the house, should walk round the estate the same day, if he can

phrases.latin: salūtārī, adpetī, dēcēdī, adsurgī, dēdūcī, redūcī, cōnsulī
phrases.english: to be greeted, sought out, made way for, stood up for, escorted there and back, consulted

sources: Lewis & Short: saluto · Lewis & Short: consaluto · Lewis & Short: resaluto
